body.text: English asks for two parts, every time
A row of words can be long, clear and still not be a sentence. English wants two things in it. This page shows you what they are.

body.gloss: a group of words that says something complete

show_first.text: The Verdon recycling centre reopens on Monday.
show_first.mark: The Verdon recycling centre reopens on Monday.

show_first.text: Rents in Ashfield rose sharply.
Most students travel by bus.

body.name_line: Each of those is a **sentence**.
body.anchor_line: Read any one of them to somebody who heard nothing before it, and they still get the message.

body.gloss: the word that says what happens or what is

show_first.text: The Brackenfield campus closes for two weeks in August.
Cyclists use the towpath every morning.
The air in Marlow is dirty.

body.name_line: That word is called the **verb**.
body.anchor_line: The third one matters. *Is* looks like nothing, and it is doing the same job as *closes*.

body.gloss: who or what the sentence is about — it comes before the verb

show_first.text: The night bus runs every forty minutes.
Fuel prices worry the drivers.
Water leaks from the old pipes.

body.name_line: That part is called the **subject**.
body.anchor_line: You have to write it. In many languages the verb ending already tells you who, so the word can be dropped. English keeps the word.

body.text: Finding the two parts in a real sentence

body.lead_in: In each one the first marked part says who or what, and the second says what happens.

items.text: The Ashfield health centre takes walk-in patients.
items.gloss: You can turn up there without booking.

items.text: Heavy traffic slows the ring road every evening.
items.gloss: Cars move slowly there at the end of the day.

items.text: My flatmate works nights at the sorting office.
items.gloss: He has a job that keeps him up at night.

items.text: Household waste in Norland has fallen by a fifth.
items.gloss: People there throw less away than they used to.

body.so_what: Long or short, each of them names something and then says what it does.

body.caption: Fill both boxes and you have a sentence.

body.text: The rule, and how short a sentence may be
Every English sentence needs a subject and a verb. In an instruction the subject is *you*, and English leaves it out.

body.lead_in: These are as short as English sentences get. Nothing has been left out of them.

items.text: Prices fell.
items.gloss: Things got cheaper. That is the whole message.

items.text: The heating works.
items.gloss: The radiators are warm today.

items.text: Two shops closed.
items.gloss: Two shops are no longer trading.

items.text: Check the timetable.
items.gloss: An instruction. The person told to do it is *you*.

body.so_what: Two words can be a whole sentence. Ten words with only one of the parts cannot.

body.text: Two ways this goes wrong

body.wrong: The long delay to the Brackenfield tram extension.
body.right: The long delay to the Brackenfield tram extension has angered residents.
body.why_it_happens: The words name something clearly and the group is long, so it feels finished. Nothing in it says what happened, so the reader is still waiting.
body.smallest_fix: Add a word that says what happens or what is: *has angered*, *continues*, *is*.

body.wrong: The tram line opened last spring passenger numbers doubled.
body.right: The tram line opened last spring. Passenger numbers doubled.
body.why_it_happens: The two facts are about one thing, so they feel like one thought. Each part has its own subject and its own verb, so each one needs its own full stop.
body.smallest_fix: Count the words that say what happens. Two of them means two sentences.

body.heard: A sentence is a group of words that expresses a complete thought.
also_known_as: a sentence is one complete idea
body.truth: That describes a sentence but it cannot test one. *The rising cost of student accommodation* feels like a complete thought, and it is not a sentence, because nothing in it says what happened.
body.what_to_do: Do not ask whether it feels finished. Look for the two parts: who or what, and what happens.

body.heard: Every sentence must have a verb and a subject, always.
also_known_as: a sentence with no subject is always wrong
body.truth: It is the right default and it is what you should write. Instructions are the one systematic gap: *Bring photo identification.* means *you bring it*, and English leaves the *you* out.
body.what_to_do: Check that every sentence you write has both parts. The only ones that need no written subject are instructions.

body.mechanism: Arabic present-tense sentences join a subject to a description directly, with no separate word doing the job of *is*.
body.wrong: The waiting room very cold.
body.right: The waiting room is very cold.
body.fix: Put *is*, *am* or *are* in, even when the sentence already feels complete.

body.mechanism: Spanish marks who is doing something on the end of the verb, so a separate subject word is not needed.
body.wrong: Is getting worse every winter.
body.right: The flooding is getting worse every winter.
body.fix: Write a subject word, even when the verb already tells you who.

body.headline: Two parts: who or what, and what happens.
points: Every English sentence needs a subject and a verb.
A long group of words with no verb is not a sentence.
*Is*, *are* and *was* are verbs, and they are not optional.
Two words that say what happens means two sentences.

articles.title: The thing the action lands on

article_json.one_line: This lets you say what was done and who it was done for, instead of only saying that something happened.
article_json.short_answer: Put the thing the action lands on straight after the verb: *The council raised the rents.* Nothing goes in between.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: Where do I put the thing the action happened to?

body.text: Some sentences need a third part
*The council decided* is a finished sentence, but it leaves the reader hanging. Many verbs want a third part: the thing they land on.

body.gloss: who or what the action lands on — it comes after the verb

show_first.text: The council raised the parking charges.
Storm damage closed the coastal path.
Our tutor marks the essays at the weekend.

body.name_line: That part is called the **object**.
body.anchor_line: In each one, ask *what?* straight after the verb. The answer is the object.

body.gloss: the person something is given to or done for

show_first.text: The landlord sent the tenants a warning letter.
The clinic offers new patients a free check-up.
My tutor lent me two of her books.

body.name_line: That part is called the **indirect object**.
body.anchor_line: It goes in front of the thing, not after it. The person comes first, then what they got.

body.text: Two ways to say who received it

body.lead_in: The same event, written both ways. Only the order and one small word change.
body.dimension: the order of the two objects

items.text: The office emailed the students the new timetable.
items.gloss: The students now have the timetable.

items.text: The office emailed the new timetable to the students.
items.gloss: Same event. The students are named at the end.

items.text: I'll send you the photos tonight.
items.gloss: The photos are coming to you later today.

items.text: The trust awarded a grant to three local schools.
items.gloss: Three schools received money from the trust.

body.so_what: Put the person first and no *to* is needed. Put the thing first and *to* or *for* has to go in.

body.text: The rule about where the object goes
The object comes straight after the verb. Nothing goes between the verb and its object.

body.lead_in: Extra information is added, and every time it waits until after the object.

items.text: The committee reviewed the plans carefully.
items.gloss: They went through the plans without rushing.

items.text: We finished the survey on Friday.
items.gloss: Friday was the day the survey was done.

items.text: She reads the news headlines every morning.
items.gloss: It is part of her daily routine.

body.so_what: In all three, the object sits against the verb and everything else waits behind it.

body.text: Where learners lose the object

body.wrong: I like very much this course.
body.right: I like this course very much.
body.why_it_happens: In many languages the describing part can slot in next to the verb. In English the object is glued to the verb, so anything else waits until after it.
body.smallest_fix: Move the describing part to the end: verb, then object, then everything else.

body.wrong: The lecturer explained us the marking system.
body.right: The lecturer explained the marking system to us.
body.why_it_happens: *Explain* looks like *tell*, and *tell* does take the person first. A small group of verbs — *explain, describe, suggest, mention, recommend* — always need *to* before the person.
body.smallest_fix: Put the thing first and add *to* before the person.

body.heard: Every English sentence is subject, verb, object.
also_known_as: English is an SVO language, so you always need three parts
body.truth: Plenty of verbs take no object at all. *The line closed.* *Rents rose.* *Nothing happened.* Adding an object to those is what makes a sentence wrong.
body.what_to_do: Ask what the verb needs. Some verbs must have an object, some cannot take one, and the dictionary marks which.

body.mechanism: Spanish attaches a short pronoun to the verb for the person receiving something, so the person naturally comes first.
body.wrong: Can you explain me the difference?
body.right: Can you explain the difference to me?
body.fix: After *explain*, *describe* and *suggest*, put the thing first and *to* before the person.

body.mechanism: Tamil marks the role of each part with an ending, so the object can sit in more than one place without confusing anybody.
body.wrong: I the report yesterday finished.
body.right: I finished the report yesterday.
body.fix: Keep the order verb, then object. English shows the role by position only.

body.headline: Verb, then object. Nothing squeezes in between.

articles.title: Sentences that describe instead of act

article_json.one_line: This lets you say what something is or is like, and explains why those sentences have no object.
article_json.short_answer: After *be*, *seem*, *become* and *look*, use a describing word, not an *-ly* word: *The results look promising.*
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How do I say what something is like?

body.text: Not every sentence has something done to it
*The rent went up* says what happened. *The rent is high* says what something is like. Nothing is done to anything in the second one, so it has no object.

body.gloss: the part that finishes off the verb and describes the subject or the object

show_first.text: The bus service is unreliable.
Her first job was a summer placement at the depot.
show_first.mark: a summer placement at the depot

show_first.text: The water in the canal looks cleaner this year.

body.name_line: That part is called the **complement**.
body.anchor_line: Each one points back at the subject and says what it is or what it is like.

body.gloss: a verb like *be*, *seem* or *become* that links a subject to a description

show_first.text: The corridor smells damp.
The queues become shorter after nine.
The plan seems expensive.

body.name_line: A verb doing that job is called a **linking verb**.
body.anchor_line: It does not do anything to the subject. It holds the subject and the description together.

body.text: Describing the subject, and describing the object

body.lead_in: The first two describe the subject. The last two describe the object instead.

items.text: The new cycle lane is narrow.
items.gloss: There is not much room on it.

items.text: My landlord is a retired engineer.
items.gloss: That is what he did before he stopped working.

items.text: The strike made the journey impossible.
items.gloss: Because of the strike, nobody could travel.

items.text: The residents called the decision unfair.
items.gloss: In their view the decision treated them badly.

body.so_what: The describing part always attaches to whatever comes just before it.

body.caption: An object receives the action. A complement describes.

body.text: The rule about the word you put after these verbs
After a linking verb, use a describing word for things, not an *-ly* word. *The results look promising*, never *promisingly*.

body.lead_in: Five linking verbs, and after every one of them a plain describing word.

items.text: The station feels unsafe after dark.
items.gloss: People do not want to wait there at night.

items.text: The coffee in the canteen tastes terrible.
items.gloss: Nobody enjoys drinking it.

items.text: Air quality in the city centre has become worse.
items.gloss: The air is dirtier than it used to be.

items.text: The building remained empty for three years.
items.gloss: Nobody used it during that time.

body.so_what: Not one of them takes an *-ly* word. The word describes the thing, not the action.

body.text: Where these sentences go wrong

body.wrong: The figures for last year looked badly.
body.right: The figures for last year looked bad.
body.why_it_happens: You were taught that *-ly* words go with verbs. *Looked* here is not an action at all, so the word after it describes the figures, not the looking.
body.smallest_fix: Ask what is being described. If it is the subject, drop the *-ly*.

body.wrong: The waiting list for the clinic very long.
body.right: The waiting list for the clinic is very long.
body.why_it_happens: The sentence already carries its meaning, so the *is* feels like a spare word. English will not join a subject to a description without a verb.
body.smallest_fix: Put *is*, *am*, *are*, *was* or *were* between the two parts.

body.heard: Never say *I feel good*. The correct form is *I feel well*.
also_known_as: *good* is an adjective so it cannot follow a verb
body.truth: *Feel* links a subject to a description, so a describing word follows it. *I feel good* is standard English. *Well* is also correct there, and it usually means *not ill*.
body.what_to_do: Use *good* for how you feel in general and *well* for health. Both are correct after *feel*.

body.mechanism: In Chinese a describing word can be the whole of what is said about a subject, with no separate linking word.
body.wrong: The rent very expensive.
body.right: The rent is very expensive.
body.fix: Put *is* or *are* in front of the describing word every time.

body.headline: Linking verb, then a describing word. No *-ly*.

articles.title: Saying when, where, why and how

article_json.one_line: This lets you add the time, the place, the reason or the manner to a sentence that already works without it.
article_json.short_answer: Add the extra part at the end, or move it to the front for emphasis. Never wedge it between the subject and the verb.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: Where do I put *yesterday*, *at the station* or *because of the rain*?

body.text: The part you can take out and still have a sentence
*The tram broke down* is complete. *The tram broke down outside the depot on Tuesday* says far more. Everything after *down* is extra, and you can remove it.

body.gloss: a piece that says how, when, where or why

show_first.text: The lifts were repaired last week.
Deliveries arrive at the back entrance.
The meeting ended early because of the weather.

body.name_line: A part doing that job is called an **adverbial**.
body.anchor_line: Cover it with your thumb. What is left is still a sentence, which is what makes it the extra part.

body.text: An adverbial can be one word, a small group, or a whole stretch with its own verb. The job is what makes it one, not the length.

body.one_line: A small word like *in*, *on*, *at* or *for* plus a noun makes one unit that places something in time or space: *at the back entrance*. The full story is in [th_prepositions_of_time].

body.text: Four questions the extra part answers

body.lead_in: One sentence, four different extra parts. Each answers a different question.

items.text: The council closed the car park on Sunday.
items.gloss: Sunday was the day it shut.

items.text: The council closed the car park behind the library.
items.gloss: That is which car park shut.

items.text: The council closed the car park without warning.
items.gloss: Nobody was told before it happened.

items.text: The council closed the car park to reduce traffic.
items.gloss: Cutting traffic was the reason for shutting it.

body.so_what: The sentence stays the same. Only the answer to *when*, *where*, *how* or *why* changes.

body.text: The rule about where this part can sit
Put the extra part at the end of the sentence, or at the front. Do not put it between the subject and the verb.

body.lead_in: The same extra part, moved from the end to the front. Both versions are correct.
body.dimension: the position of the extra part

items.text: Rents have risen fastest in the coastal towns.
items.gloss: Coastal towns saw the biggest increases.

items.text: In the coastal towns, rents have risen fastest.
items.gloss: Same fact. The place is what the reader meets first.

items.text: We check the water levels every morning.
items.gloss: It is a daily job.

items.text: Every morning we check the water levels.
items.gloss: Same job. The routine is what the reader meets first.

body.so_what: Moving it changes what the reader notices first. It does not change what happened.

body.text: Two things that go wrong with the extra part

body.wrong: I yesterday evening finished the report.
body.right: I finished the report yesterday evening.
body.why_it_happens: Many languages put the time in front of the verb, and it feels like the natural slot. English keeps the subject and the verb together.
body.smallest_fix: Move the time part to the end, or put it right at the front.

body.wrong: The driver took the corner careful.
body.right: The driver took the corner carefully.
body.why_it_happens: The word describes a person, so the plain describing word feels right. It is telling you how the driving was done, so it needs the *-ly* ending.
body.smallest_fix: If it answers *how?*, add *-ly*.

body.heard: Extra information always goes at the end of the sentence.
also_known_as: time and place always come last
body.truth: The end is the usual place, and the front is available whenever you want the reader to meet the time or the place first. *On Tuesday the depot reopened* is standard written English.
body.what_to_do: Use the end by default. Move it to the front when the time or the place is what links this sentence to the one before.

body.mechanism: Chinese puts time and place words in front of the verb, so they naturally land between the subject and the verb in English.
body.wrong: She on Monday sent the application.
body.right: She sent the application on Monday.
body.fix: Keep the subject and verb together. Send the time part to the end or the front.

body.headline: End by default. Front for emphasis. Never in the middle.

articles.title: Word groups with a verb, and word groups without

article_json.also_called: Clause and phrase; main and subordinate clauses
article_json.one_line: This gives you the one test that the rest of this reference relies on, so every later page can be read.
article_json.short_answer: Look inside the group for something doing something. Found it, that is a clause. Not there, that is a phrase.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: What is the difference between a clause and a phrase?

body.text: Two words the rest of this reference cannot do without
Almost every grammar book uses these two words on page one and never explains them. This page gives you a test you can run in two seconds.

body.gloss: a group of words with its own subject and its own verb

show_first.text: The library closes at six because staff numbers were cut.
Nobody knew that the platform had been moved.
When the ferry docks, the traffic backs up.

body.name_line: Each marked group is a **clause**.
body.anchor_line: Look inside each one. There is something being talked about, and something it does.

body.gloss: a small group of words that works as one unit and has no verb in it

show_first.text: The library closes at six because of staff cuts.
Nobody knew about the change of platform.
After the ferry, the traffic backs up.

body.name_line: Each marked group is a **phrase**.
body.anchor_line: Nothing inside them is doing anything. They name a thing or place a thing, and then they stop.

body.text: The two-second test, run on real groups
Look inside the group for something doing something. If it is there, the group is a clause. If it is not, the group is a phrase.

body.lead_in: Seven groups of words. In each one, ask whether something inside is doing something.
body.dimension: does it contain a doer and a verb

items.text: after the storm
items.gloss: Nothing is doing anything here. It is a phrase.

items.text: after the storm hit the coast
items.gloss: The storm hit. That is a doer and a verb, so it is a clause.

items.text: the rising cost of childcare
items.gloss: A thing is named and nothing happens to it. A phrase.

items.text: childcare costs are rising
items.gloss: Costs are doing something, so this is a clause.

items.text: in a badly lit underpass near the station
items.gloss: Long, and still only a place. A phrase.

items.text: she left
items.gloss: Two words, a doer and a verb. A clause.

items.text: hoping for a quick answer
items.gloss: There is no doer inside it, so it is a phrase.

body.so_what: Length has nothing to do with it. A two-word clause beats a nine-word phrase.

body.text: Some clauses stand alone and some cannot

body.gloss: the part that can stand on its own

show_first.text: The pool reopened after the repairs were finished.
Although the fare went up, passenger numbers held steady.

body.name_line: The marked part is the **main clause**.
body.anchor_line: Say the marked part on its own and nobody is left waiting. That is the test.

body.gloss: the part that cannot stand on its own

show_first.text: The pool reopened after the repairs were finished.
Although the fare went up, passenger numbers held steady.

body.name_line: The marked part is the **subordinate clause**.
body.anchor_line: It has a doer and a verb, so it is a clause. The word at its front leaves the listener waiting for more.

body.lead_in: Each subordinate clause is marked. Read it alone and hear how it hangs.
body.dimension: the clause that cannot stand alone

items.text: The scheme was dropped because the funding ran out.

body.so_what: Each marked part has a doer and a verb, and none of them can be a sentence on its own.

body.text: Which joining word takes a clause, and which takes a phrase

body.question: Does the part after the joining word contain a doer and a verb?

options.label: a clause word
options.use_it_when: The part after it has its own doer and verb: *although*, *because*, *while*, *after*, *when*.
options.example: Although the work overran, the road reopened on time.

options.label: a phrase word
options.use_it_when: The part after it names a thing and nothing more: *despite*, *because of*, *during*, *after*.
options.example: Despite the overrun, the road reopened on time.

a.text: Despite the delay, the team finished the survey.
a.means: The survey got done, and the delay did not stop it.

b.text: Although the work was delayed, the team finished the survey.
b.means: The same outcome, with the hold-up spelled out as an event.

minimal_pairs.only_difference: Despite the delay / Although the work was delayed

a.text: Because of the strike, no trains ran on Tuesday.
a.means: A strike stopped the trains that day.

b.text: Because the drivers walked out, no trains ran on Tuesday.

minimal_pairs.only_difference: Because of the strike / Because the drivers walked out

b.text: While the repairs were going on, the library moved into a portable building.

b.span: While the repairs were going on

minimal_pairs.only_difference: During the repairs / While the repairs were going on

body.deciding_factor: Read what follows the joining word. If something in it is doing something, you need the clause word.
body.trap: *Despite* and *although* translate to the same word in many languages, so they feel interchangeable. They take different kinds of word group.
body.register_note: Both belong in speech and in writing. The choice pays most in Task 2, where the contrast sentence is where this error shows up.

body.wrong: Despite the buses were late, most people arrived on time.
body.right: Although the buses were late, most people arrived on time.
body.why_it_happens: *Despite* and *although* carry the same meaning, so either one feels available. *Despite* can only be followed by a named thing, never by a doer and a verb.
body.smallest_fix: Swap *despite* for *although*, or cut the sentence back to *despite the late buses*.

body.wrong: Although the funding was approved in March.
body.right: Although the funding was approved in March, the work has not started.
body.why_it_happens: The group has a doer and a verb, so it feels like a sentence. *Although* at the front makes it a part, and a part needs the rest of the sentence with it.
body.smallest_fix: Add the part that can stand on its own, or delete *although*.

body.heard: A phrase is a short group of words and a clause is a long one.
also_known_as: a clause is basically half a sentence
body.truth: Length decides nothing. *She left* is two words and it is a clause. *In a badly lit underpass near the station* is eight words and it is a phrase, because nothing in it is doing anything.
body.what_to_do: Ignore length. Look inside the group for something doing something.

body.mechanism: Arabic written style joins many clauses in a long chain, and the reader is expected to follow the chain rather than the full stops.
body.wrong: The funding was approved and the work started and the road reopened and traffic improved.
body.right: The funding was approved, so the work started. The road reopened and traffic improved.
body.fix: Count the clauses. Two or three in one sentence is the English written limit.

articles.title: Verbs that carry a time, and verbs that do not

article_json.one_line: This explains why some verb forms can hold a sentence up on their own and others never can.
article_json.short_answer: Ask whether the verb tells you *when*. *Runs* and *ran* do, so they can hold a sentence up. *To run* and *running* do not.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: Why is *working late every night* not a sentence?

body.text: Some verb forms tell you when, and some do not
*The clinic opens at eight* tells you the opening happens now, as a habit. *To open at eight* tells you nothing about when. Both contain the same verb.

body.gloss: a verb with a time on it: *goes*, *went*

show_first.text: The recycling centre opens on Saturdays.
Two of the bridges closed for repairs.
The waiting list is getting longer.

body.name_line: A verb with a time on it is called a **finite verb**.
body.anchor_line: Change the marked word and the time of the whole sentence changes with it. That is what makes it the one holding the sentence up.

body.gloss: a verb with no time on it: *to go*, *going*, *gone*

show_first.text: The council hopes to reopen the pool.
Cycling to work saves an hour a day.
Damaged by the flood, the hall stayed shut.

body.name_line: A verb form with no time on it is called a **non-finite verb**.
body.anchor_line: None of the marked words tells you when. The time is carried by the other verb in the sentence.

body.text: Why this matters for your full stops
A sentence needs at least one verb with a time on it. *To go*, *going* and *gone* can never do that job alone.

body.lead_in: Three groups with a verb in them, and only the third one is a sentence.
body.dimension: whether the verb carries a time

items.text: Working late every night for a month.
items.gloss: Not a sentence. Nothing here tells you when it happened.

items.text: To finish the survey before the deadline.
items.gloss: Not a sentence either. It names a plan and stops.

items.text: The team worked late every night for a month.
items.gloss: A sentence. *Worked* puts it in the past.

items.text: She's hoping to finish before the deadline.
items.gloss: A sentence. *'s hoping* carries the time; *to finish* carries none.

body.so_what: Every one of them contains a verb. Only the ones with a time on the verb are sentences.

body.caption: One verb carries the time. The others hang off it.

spec.caption: Only the middle box changes when the time changes.

body.lead_in: The same sentence at three different times. Watch which word moves.

items.text: The trust plans to fund two new clinics.
items.gloss: That is the plan as things stand.

items.text: The trust planned to fund two new clinics.
items.gloss: That was the plan at some point in the past.

items.text: The trust is planning to fund two new clinics.
items.gloss: The planning is going on at the moment.

body.so_what: *To fund* never moved. Only the first verb carries the time.

body.text: Two errors this explains

body.wrong: The residents' group meeting the planners next Tuesday.
body.right: The residents' group is meeting the planners next Tuesday.
body.why_it_happens: *Meeting* is a verb form and *next Tuesday* names a time, so the group looks finished. Nothing in it carries a time on the verb itself.
body.smallest_fix: Add *is*, *was* or *will be* in front of the *-ing* word.

body.wrong: The committee decided to reviewed the whole scheme.
body.right: The committee decided to review the whole scheme.
body.why_it_happens: The sentence is about the past, so the past ending gets attached to both verbs. Only the first verb in the group carries the time.
body.smallest_fix: After *to*, use the plain form of the verb with no ending.

body.heard: Any word ending in *-ing* is a verb.
body.truth: An *-ing* word carries no time at all. It can name an activity, as in *Cycling saves money*, or describe a thing, as in *the rising cost*. Only a helper in front of it puts it in a time.
body.what_to_do: When you see an *-ing* word, look for a helper such as *is*, *was* or *has been*. Without one, no time is being stated.

body.mechanism: Hindi builds long sentences by chaining verb forms that carry no time, and marks the time once at the very end.
body.wrong: Having checked the figures and sending the report.
body.right: Having checked the figures, she sent the report.
body.fix: Make sure one verb in the sentence carries a time, and give it a subject.

body.text: The same word can do two different jobs
*The rise in fares was steep.* *Fares rise every January.* The word *rise* is a thing in the first sentence and something happening in the second.
So a word class is a job, not a label stuck to a word for life. Two tests tell you which job a word is doing here.

body.gloss: a word for a person, a thing, a place or an idea

show_first.text: The nurse checked the equipment.

body.name_line: A word doing that job is called a **noun**.
body.anchor_line: Two of those you can touch. *Decision* you cannot, and it is still a noun, because it names something.

body.gloss: one / more than one

show_first.text: One bridge was closed for repairs.
Four bridges were closed for repairs.
The volunteers cleared three footpaths.

body.name_line: One is **singular** and more than one is **plural**.
body.anchor_line: The *-s* is not optional in English. A number in front of the noun does not do the job for you.

body.text: Two tests you can run on any word
If *the* fits in front of it and it can take an *-s*, it is a noun. If you can move it in time, it is a verb.

body.lead_in: One word, tested twice. The same shape does both jobs.

items.gloss: Trains going north are held up.

body.so_what: *The* fits in front of the first and third. The second and fourth moved in time.

body.text: Number words behave like the words in front of nouns

body.lead_in: English uses three kinds of number word, and they sit in different places:
items: counting numbers, in front of a plural noun: *three platforms*
position numbers, after *the*: *the third platform*
shares of a whole, before *of*: *a quarter of the intake*

body.lead_in: The three kinds of number word, each in a sentence.

items.text: Four of the six lifts were out of service.
items.gloss: Only two lifts were working.

items.text: The second phase of the project starts in April.
items.gloss: There is an earlier phase, and it is already under way.

items.text: About a third of the students live at home.
items.gloss: Roughly one student in three does not move out.

body.so_what: A counting number takes a plural noun. A position number needs *the* in front of it.

body.text: Two errors that come from the wrong word class

body.wrong: Three of the machine broke down in the same week.
body.right: Three of the machines broke down in the same week.
body.why_it_happens: *Three* already says how many, so the *-s* looks like the same information twice. English marks the number in both places.
body.smallest_fix: After a number or after *many*, add *-s* to the noun.

body.wrong: The council will announcement the results in June.
body.right: The council will announce the results in June.
body.why_it_happens: *Announcement* and *announce* carry the same meaning, so either one feels usable. Only the verb can follow a helper such as *will*.
body.smallest_fix: After *will*, *can*, *must* or *to*, use the plain verb with no ending.

body.heard: A noun is a person, a place or a thing.
also_known_as: if you cannot touch it, it is not a noun
body.truth: That covers most nouns and leaves out the ones that matter for essay writing. *Pollution*, *delay*, *evidence* and *decision* name no object you can hold, and every one of them is a noun.
body.what_to_do: Use the test instead of the list. If *the* fits in front of it, it is a noun.

body.mechanism: Chinese carries number in the number word and the measure word, so the noun itself never changes shape.
body.wrong: The college offers five course in the evening.
body.right: The college offers five courses in the evening.
body.fix: Add *-s* to the noun as well as using the number.

articles.title: Words that describe things, and words that describe actions

article_json.one_line: This tells you which of two very similar words a slot needs, and why the *-ly* test lets you down.
article_json.short_answer: Describing a thing, use the plain word: *a quick decision*. Describing an action, add *-ly*: *decided quickly*.

body.text: Two describing jobs, and they are not the same
One kind of word describes a thing. The other says how, when or where something is done. English keeps them apart, and often the only sign is an ending.

body.gloss: a word that describes a noun

show_first.text: The new footbridge takes two minutes to cross.
Rents in the city are unaffordable for most graduates.
A heavy lorry blocked the lane for an hour.

body.name_line: A word doing that job is called an **adjective**.
body.anchor_line: It sits in front of the thing, or after *be*, *seem* and *look*. It never takes an *-s*, however many things there are.

body.gloss: a word that says how, when or where something happens

show_first.text: The queue moved slowly.
The results were published yesterday.
The report was genuinely useful.

body.name_line: A word doing that job is called an **adverb**.
body.anchor_line: The last one describes another describing word, not a verb. That is normal, and it is why the usual definition is too narrow.

body.text: Which one does this slot need?

body.question: Am I describing a thing, or how something is done?

options.label: the plain word
options.use_it_when: It describes a thing: in front of the noun, or after *be*, *seem*, *look*, *feel*, *become*.
options.example: The team made a quick decision.

options.label: the *-ly* word
options.use_it_when: It says how, when or where something happened, or it sharpens another describing word.

body.deciding_factor: Ask what the word tells you about. A thing takes the plain word; an action takes the *-ly* word.
body.trap: You were taught that adverbs end in *-ly*, so *fast*, *hard* and *late* look like the wrong class and *friendly* looks like the right one.
body.register_note: The choice matters in both speech and writing. In Task 1 it decides between *a sharp rise* and *rose sharply*, which are both useful and not interchangeable.

body.text: The *-ly* test fails in both directions, so it is not worth trusting. Ask what the word describes instead, because that never lets you down.

body.caption: Some adverbs have no *-ly*, and some *-ly* words describe things.
footnotes: There is no *-ly* form of *friendly*. Say *in a friendly way* instead.

body.text: Use the plain word when it describes a thing. Use the *-ly* word when it says how, when or where something happens.

items.gloss: Far fewer people came, and the drop was sudden.

items.gloss: Somebody took their time and got it right.

items.gloss: Nothing was skipped over.

body.text: Where the wrong form slips in

body.wrong: The new booking system works good.
body.right: The new booking system works well.
body.why_it_happens: *Good* is the word you reach for, and it is the right one after *be* and *seem*. *Works* is an action, so it needs the form that describes actions.
body.smallest_fix: After an action verb use *well*. After *be*, *seem* or *look*, *good* is correct.

body.wrong: There are three differents routes into the city.
body.right: There are three different routes into the city.
body.why_it_happens: In many languages a describing word matches the noun for number, so the *-s* transfers across. English adjectives never change shape.
body.smallest_fix: Take the *-s* off the describing word. Only the noun carries it.

body.heard: Adverbs end in *-ly*, and adjectives do not.
also_known_as: if it ends in *-ly* it describes a verb
body.truth: Both halves fail. *Fast*, *hard*, *late*, *early* and *well* describe actions and have no *-ly*. *Friendly*, *likely*, *costly* and *lonely* describe things and do end in *-ly*.
body.what_to_do: Do not look at the ending. Ask whether the word is describing a thing or an action, and choose from that.

body.mechanism: Spanish describing words change their ending to match the noun for number and gender, and they usually follow the noun.
body.wrong: We visited two museums olds.
body.right: We visited two old museums.
body.fix: Put the describing word in front of the noun and leave its ending alone.

articles.title: Words that stand in for a noun, and words that go in front of one

article_json.one_line: This separates the small words that replace a noun from the small words that must sit in front of one.

body.text: Replacing a noun, and introducing one
Two families of small words cluster around nouns. One family stands where the noun would have been. The other family goes in front of the noun and stays there.

body.gloss: a word that stands in for a noun

show_first.text: The lift broke down again, and it took two days to fix.
The tenants met the landlord, but he refused to listen.
My neighbours moved out because they could not pay the rent.

body.name_line: A word doing that job is called a **pronoun**.
body.anchor_line: Each one saves you repeating a noun you have already used. The reader has to be able to tell which noun it stands for.

body.gloss: the word before a noun that says which one or how many

show_first.text: This platform is closed until Monday.
Some passengers waited over an hour.
My season ticket runs out in June.

body.name_line: A word doing that job is called a **determiner**.
body.anchor_line: Only one of them can go in front of a noun at a time. *The my ticket* is not available in English.

body.gloss: the little word *a*, *an* or *the* in front of a noun

show_first.text: A cyclist was hurt at the junction.

The inspector found two faults.

body.name_line: Those three words are called **articles**.
body.anchor_line: *A* introduces one of many. *The* points at one you and your reader can both identify.

body.text: The rule about how many can go in front
One word goes in front of a noun to say which one. Choosing *my* means you cannot also use *the*.

items.gloss: It belongs to the person speaking.

items.gloss: Not one of them got through.

body.so_what: The noun never moved. The word in front of it changed who or which one you meant.

items.gloss: The scheme is her responsibility.

items.text: The trustees asked her to stay on.
items.gloss: They wanted her to keep doing it.

items.text: Her report goes to the board next week.

body.so_what: Nothing about the person changed. The slot decided the shape of the word.

body.text: Two things that go wrong with these small words

body.wrong: She works as receptionist at the health centre.
body.right: She works as a receptionist at the health centre.
body.why_it_happens: The sentence is clear without it, and many languages leave the slot empty. A singular noun in English almost always needs a word in front of it.
body.smallest_fix: Put *a*, *an*, *the*, *my* or *this* in front of the singular noun.

body.wrong: My supervisor she has approved the change.
body.right: My supervisor has approved the change.
body.why_it_happens: Many languages restate the subject with a short word for emphasis. In English the noun and the stand-in word are two ways of doing one job, so only one of them goes in.
body.smallest_fix: Delete the stand-in word when the noun is already there.

body.heard: A pronoun always stands for the noun immediately before it.
also_known_as: *it* refers to the last thing mentioned
body.truth: A reader looks for the nearest noun that fits, and if two of them fit, the sentence is unclear. *The council told the contractor that it had run out of money* leaves two possible owners of the money.
body.what_to_do: Read your sentence back and ask which noun each stand-in word points to. If two could fit, repeat the noun.

body.mechanism: Russian has no *a* or *the*. Whether a thing is already known is shown by word order and by context instead.
body.wrong: Student handed in report on Friday.
body.right: The student handed in her report on Friday.
body.fix: Ask whether the reader already knows which one. Yes, use *the*. No, use *a*.

article_json.also_called: Prepositions, conjunctions and the words that stand outside the sentence
article_json.one_line: This separates the small words that place something in time or space from the ones that join two parts together.
article_json.short_answer: A preposition is followed by a thing: *in March*. A conjunction is followed by a part of the sentence: *because it rained*.

body.text: Both families are small words, and they behave differently
*In*, *because* and *although* are all short words that hold a sentence together. What follows them is not the same in each case, and that is the whole difference.

body.gloss: a small word that places something in time or space: *in*, *on*, *at*, *for*

show_first.text: The recycling point is behind the supermarket.

The town has been without a bank since March.

body.name_line: A word doing that job is called a **preposition**.
body.anchor_line: A noun always comes after it. Take the noun away and the sentence stops making sense.

show_first.text: The road was resurfaced and the drains were cleared.
The scheme was approved but the money never arrived.

body.name_line: A word doing that job is called a **conjunction**.
body.anchor_line: What follows each one has its own doer and its own verb. That is what makes it a joining word and not a placing word.

body.text: The rule that tells the two families apart
A preposition is followed by a thing. A conjunction is followed by a group with its own doer and verb.

body.lead_in: Four pairs of words that mean nearly the same and take different things after them.

items.text: The class was cancelled because of the snow.

body.so_what: The first of each pair is followed by a thing. The second is followed by something doing something.

body.caption: Same meaning, different family, so different word.
footnotes: *Before* and *after* belong to both families, so they never need changing.
*Due to* is safest after a form of *be*: *the delay was due to flooding*.

body.text: The words that sit outside the sentence
A third group belongs to neither family. *Oh*, *well*, *right* and *anyway* are attached to nothing, and they help a conversation move along.

items.text: Well, the deadline has moved again.
items.gloss: The speaker is easing into news the listener will not like.

items.text: Right, let's look at the figures.
items.gloss: The speaker is starting a new part of the meeting.

items.text: Anyway, the trains are running normally today.
items.gloss: The speaker is going back to the main subject.

body.so_what: Take any of them out and the sentence is untouched. That is what puts them outside it.

Two errors these families produce

body.wrong: Although the fare rose, but passenger numbers held up.
body.right: Although the fare rose, passenger numbers held up.
body.why_it_happens: Several languages mark a contrast at both ends, so both words feel necessary. English marks it once, at the front or in the middle.
body.smallest_fix: Delete one of them. Keep *although* at the front, or keep *but* in the middle.

body.wrong: The committee discussed about the parking proposals.
body.right: The committee discussed the parking proposals.
body.why_it_happens: *Talk about* takes a preposition, so *discuss* looks as though it should too. Which preposition a verb takes, or takes none at all, is fixed for each verb.
body.smallest_fix: *Discuss*, *enter*, *reach*, *contact* and *approach* take no preposition.

body.heard: A joining word has to go in the middle, between the two parts it joins.
also_known_as: you cannot start a sentence with a joining word
body.truth: *Because*, *although*, *if*, *when* and *while* work from the front just as well. *Although the pitch was soft, the match went ahead* is standard written English, and the comma marks the join.
body.what_to_do: Put the joining word wherever the emphasis needs it. Check that the sentence still has a part that could stand on its own.

body.mechanism: Chinese marks a contrast or a reason with a pair of words, one at the front of each part, and both are needed.
body.wrong: Because the bus was late, so I missed the class.
body.right: Because the bus was late, I missed the class.
body.fix: Use one joining word per join. Choose the front one or the middle one.

In *she has finished*, only *finished* names the event. *Has* is there to build the shape. English has a small set of verbs that do that job.

body.name_line: A verb doing that job is called a **modal verb**.
body.anchor_line: Take the marked word out and the event stays the same. What changes is how necessary, how likely or how advisable it is.

body.text: The nine words in the second family

body.lead_in: There are nine of these, and this is the whole list:
items: *can*, *could*
*may*, *might*
*will*, *would*
*shall*, *should*
*must*

body.text: The list is closed, so nothing is ever added to it. That is why they are worth learning as a set.
The rule about what comes after one of these nine
After one of the nine, use the plain verb. No *to*, no *-s*, no *-ing* and no past ending.

body.lead_in: Four subjects, one modal verb. Watch what does not change.

items.text: I must renew the permit this week.
items.gloss: There is no way round it for me.

items.text: She must renew the permit this week.
items.gloss: The same obligation, on somebody else.

items.text: The tenants must renew their permits this week.
items.gloss: It applies to all of them.

items.text: You must renew it before Friday, or you'll be fined.
items.gloss: There is a penalty for leaving it too late.

body.so_what: The subject changed four times. Neither verb changed shape once.

body.caption: Helper first, then the main verb. The helper carries everything.

spec.caption: Only the middle box changes for a question or a negative.

body.lead_in: One statement turned into a negative and a question. Only the helper moves.

items.text: The engineers have checked the pumps.
items.gloss: The pumps have been looked at.

items.text: The engineers have not checked the pumps.
items.gloss: The pumps are still waiting.

items.text: Have the engineers checked the pumps?
items.gloss: You are asking whether the job is done.

body.so_what: *Checked* did not move. The helper took the *not* and then went to the front.

body.text: Two errors that come from this family

body.wrong: Applicants must to provide two references.
body.right: Applicants must provide two references.
body.why_it_happens: *Have to* and *need to* both contain *to*, and they mean much the same as *must*. The nine take the plain verb and nothing else.
body.smallest_fix: Delete *to* after *can*, *could*, *may*, *might*, *will*, *would*, *shall*, *should* and *must*.

body.wrong: The office did not received the form.
body.right: The office did not receive the form.
body.why_it_happens: The sentence is about the past, so the past ending gets put on the main verb as well. *Did* is already carrying the time for the whole group.
body.smallest_fix: After *did*, put the main verb back to its plain form.

body.heard: *Do* is only used to make questions and negatives.
body.truth: *Do* is also an ordinary verb with a meaning of its own: *We do the stock check on Fridays.* It also adds force to a statement: *I did send the form.*
body.what_to_do: Read what *do* is doing in the sentence. If a main verb follows it, *do* is helping; if not, *do* is the main verb.

body.mechanism: Spanish makes a negative with one word in front of the verb and a question by intonation alone, so no helper is needed.
body.wrong: You like the new timetable?
body.right: Do you like the new timetable?
body.fix: Build a question with a helper at the front. In writing, intonation is not available.

article_json.one_line: This shows you how to turn a verb into a noun and back, so one idea gives you four usable words.
article_json.short_answer: Change the ending to change the word class: *decide* becomes *decision*. Change the beginning to change the meaning: *possible* becomes *impossible*.

body.text: One idea, four words, one slot each
*Decide*, *decision*, *decisive*, *decisively*. They carry one meaning between them, and the sentence decides which one you need. Grammar owns the mechanism; the words themselves are vocabulary.
Two things can change. An ending changes the job the word does, so the sentence has to be rebuilt round it. A beginning changes the meaning and leaves the job alone.

body.gloss: a piece added at the start / at the end of a word that changes it

show_first.text: The plan was unworkable from the start.
Enrolment closed at the end of August.
They had to reschedule the inspection.

body.name_line: A piece at the start is a **prefix** and a piece at the end is a **suffix**.
body.anchor_line: Cover the marked piece and a shorter word is left underneath. That is the word the ending or the beginning was added to.

body.text: Endings that change the job the word does

body.caption: Each ending moves a word into a different job.
footnotes: Which ending a word takes is fixed. *Decide* takes *-sion* and there is no *decidement*.

body.lead_in: One idea in four slots. Watch how the sentence rebuilds itself each time.
body.dimension: the job the word is doing

items.text: The panel decided against the new route.
items.gloss: They said no to it.

items.text: The panel's decision angered local residents.
items.gloss: People living nearby were unhappy about it.

items.text: She was decisive at the meeting.
items.gloss: She made her mind up and said so.

items.text: They acted decisively once the report came out.
items.gloss: They moved fast and did not hesitate.

body.so_what: The idea never changed. The slot in the sentence decided which shape it took.

body.text: Some words change job with no ending at all
A large group of English words move between jobs without changing shape. This is why a dictionary lists the same spelling twice.

body.lead_in: Three words, each used as a thing and then as something happening.
body.dimension: the job of an unchanged word

items.text: There was a sharp rise in cycling last year.
items.gloss: More people cycled than before.

items.text: Cycling numbers rise every spring.
items.gloss: It happens each year when the weather improves.

items.text: We're waiting on a report from the surveyor.
items.gloss: The surveyor has not sent it yet.

items.text: Residents report the same problem every winter.
items.gloss: They tell the council about it each year.

body.so_what: The spelling is identical. Only the slot tells you which job the word has.

body.text: Beginnings that change the meaning
A beginning changes the meaning and leaves the job alone. *Possible* and *impossible* both describe things.

body.caption: Six beginnings, and what each one does to the meaning.
footnotes: Which of *un-*, *in-*, *im-*, *il-* and *ir-* a word takes is fixed by the word, not chosen by you.

body.lead_in: The same word with three different beginnings. Only the meaning moves.

items.text: The bus service in Norland is underused.
items.gloss: Buses run, and hardly anybody is on them.

items.text: The car park is overused at weekends.
items.gloss: Too many cars try to get in on a Saturday.

items.text: The old ticket machines are unused now.
items.gloss: Nobody uses them at all any more.

body.so_what: The job of the word stayed the same in all three. Only how much use changed.

body.text: Three errors this produces

body.wrong: The develop of the site took ten years.
body.right: The development of the site took ten years.
body.why_it_happens: *The* signals that a naming word is coming, and the shorter form is the one you know best. After *the*, the word has to be in its naming shape.
body.smallest_fix: After *the*, *a* or *this*, use the form with the naming ending.

body.wrong: Rebuilding the pier by March would be unpossible.
body.right: Rebuilding the pier by March would be impossible.
body.why_it_happens: *Un-* is the commonest of the five, so it gets applied to everything. Each word takes one of them and only one.
body.smallest_fix: Check the word in a dictionary. *Un-* is the default and it is wrong often enough to be worth checking.

body.wrong: The economical situation has worsened since 2019.
body.right: The economic situation has worsened since 2019.
body.why_it_happens: Both endings exist on the same base word, so either looks available. *Economic* means to do with the economy; *economical* means cheap to run.
body.smallest_fix: Learn the pair. *Historic* and *historical*, *classic* and *classical* work the same way.

body.heard: *Un-* is the negative beginning. Put it on any word to make the opposite.
body.truth: English has five of them and each word takes a fixed one. *Unsafe* is right, *impossible* is right, *illegal* is right, *irregular* is right, and none of them swap.
body.what_to_do: Treat the negative form as a separate word to learn, not as something you build. Check it if you are not sure.

body.mechanism: Tamil builds long words by stacking endings, and one word can carry what English spreads over several.
body.wrong: The council announced the improve of the junction.
body.right: The council announced the improvement of the junction.
body.fix: After *the*, use the naming shape of the word, with its ending in place.

body.text: A slot can hold one word or twelve
*Rents rose.* *The average rent for a one-bedroom flat in the city centre rose.* The subject slot is the same size in both. It is just fuller in the second one.
That is where academic density comes from. Band 6 writing puts one word in each slot, so it needs more sentences to carry the same information.

body.text: Trimmings go in front of the head, and behind it
Single describing words go in front of the head. Anything longer goes behind it.

body.text: Two errors that come from long groups

body.wrong: The list of approved suppliers have been updated.
body.right: The list of approved suppliers has been updated.
body.why_it_happens: *Suppliers* is the word nearest the verb and it is plural, so the plural verb sounds right. The head of the group is *list*, and the head is what the verb matches.
body.smallest_fix: Strip the trimmings off the subject. Match the verb to what is left.

body.wrong: The council announced a five-years regeneration plan.
body.right: The council announced a five-year regeneration plan.
body.why_it_happens: Five years is more than one, so the *-s* looks obligatory. In front of the head the words act as description, and description never takes a plural ending.
body.smallest_fix: Drop the *-s* from anything sitting in front of the head.

body.heard: The subject of a sentence is the noun closest to the verb.
also_known_as: match the verb to the nearest word
body.truth: The subject is the whole group, and the head of that group decides the verb. In *the list of approved suppliers*, the head is *list*, so the verb is singular however many suppliers there are.
body.what_to_do: Cover everything after the head and read the sentence again. What you can still hear is what the verb has to match.

body.mechanism: Arabic places most description after the noun, so the long front-loaded English group has to be built in the opposite order.
body.wrong: The plan regeneration five-year was announced.
body.right: The five-year regeneration plan was announced.
body.fix: Single describing words go in front of the head. Only longer stretches go behind it.

articles.title: The seven shapes an English clause takes

article_json.also_called: Clause patterns: SV, SVO, SVC, SVOO, SVOC, SVA, SVOA
article_json.one_line: This lays out every shape an English clause can have, so you can see which parts a verb still needs.
article_json.short_answer: Seven shapes, and the verb chooses. *The line closed* needs nothing more; *she put the files* needs a place.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: How many parts does this sentence still need?

body.text: The verb decides what the rest of the clause looks like
Every English clause has a subject and a verb. What comes after the verb is not free. The verb itself decides, and there are seven possible answers.
Knowing the seven is useful for one thing above all: it tells you whether a sentence you have written is actually finished.

body.caption: Seven shapes. The verb picks one and the sentence has to supply the parts.
rows: what something is or is like
We sent the council a letter.
something was made a certain way
The delay made the plan unworkable.
The parcel went to the wrong depot.
She put the files in the archive.
footnotes: The last two are the shapes references usually leave out, and they are why *She put the files* sounds unfinished.

body.lead_in: One shape per example, in the order of the table above.

items.text: Two of the ferries broke down.
items.gloss: They stopped working and nothing else is being said.

items.text: Strong winds cancelled the afternoon crossings.
items.gloss: The wind stopped the boats sailing.

items.text: The waiting room is freezing.
items.gloss: It is very cold in there.

items.text: The office sent the students a reminder.
items.gloss: The students got a message telling them to act.

items.text: The strike made the timetable meaningless.
items.gloss: Nobody could rely on the published times.

items.text: The application went to the wrong department.
items.gloss: It reached a department that could not deal with it.

items.text: He left his pass on the train.
items.gloss: The pass is still on the train and he is not.

body.so_what: Each one is finished. Take the part after the verb away and most of them stop making sense.

body.text: Some verbs need a where, not just an object
*Put*, *place*, *lay* and *stand* will not let you stop after the object. Something has to say where, because the meaning is incomplete without it.
Check what the verb still needs. *Put* needs an object and a place. *Close* needs an object or nothing.

body.lead_in: Three verbs that will not release you until a place is added.

items.text: The porter put the boxes in the storeroom.
items.gloss: The boxes are in the storeroom now.

items.text: They placed the recycling bins beside the entrance.
items.gloss: Anyone coming in walks straight past the bins.

items.text: I've left my bag under the desk.
items.gloss: The bag is still under the desk.

body.so_what: Delete the marked part in any of them and the reader is left waiting.

body.text: Three things that go wrong with these shapes

body.wrong: The technician put the spare parts.
body.right: The technician put the spare parts in the van.
body.why_it_happens: The object is there, so the sentence looks complete against the commonest shape. *Put* is one of the verbs that needs a place as well.
body.smallest_fix: Add a where part after the object, or change the verb to *stored* or *kept*.

body.wrong: The heavy rain happened a lot of damage.
body.right: The heavy rain caused a lot of damage.
body.why_it_happens: *Happen* feels like an action done to something, so an object seems natural. *Happen* never takes one, and *cause* does.
body.smallest_fix: Swap in a verb that takes an object: *caused*, *produced*, *led to*.

body.wrong: The delegation arrived the conference centre at ten.
body.right: The delegation arrived at the conference centre at ten.
body.why_it_happens: *Reach* takes a plain object, so *arrive* looks as though it should too. *Arrive* takes a place part, and a place part needs its small word.
body.smallest_fix: Use *arrive at* for a point and *arrive in* for a town or country.

body.heard: Any verb can be used in any of these patterns.
also_known_as: English word order is free once you know subject, verb, object
body.truth: Each verb allows only the shapes its meaning permits, and the dictionary lists them. *Disappear* allows no object; *put* demands an object and a place; *give* allows two orders.
body.what_to_do: When a sentence sounds odd, check what the verb needs rather than moving words around.

body.mechanism: Russian marks the role of each part with an ending, so the parts can be reordered and the meaning stays fixed.
body.wrong: Arrived yesterday to the depot two inspectors.
body.right: Two inspectors arrived at the depot yesterday.
body.fix: Put the subject first, then the verb, then whatever the verb needs.

body.text: Three kinds of verb, and they behave differently
Some verbs act on something. Some never do. A third group does neither: it holds a subject and a description together, and it is the group that causes the most trouble.

The old warehouse collapsed overnight.

body.name_line: The first and third are **transitive** and the second is **intransitive**.

body.text: The linking verbs, in full
This list is closed. Fourteen verbs can hold a subject and a description together, and no others do it.

body.lead_in: These fourteen verbs take a describing word, not an *-ly* word:
items: *be*, *seem*, *appear*
*become*, *get*, *turn*, *grow*, *go*
*remain*, *stay*, *keep*
*look*, *sound*, *feel*, *taste*, *smell*

body.text: Several of them also work as ordinary action verbs. When they do, the *-ly* word is correct again, and the meaning is different.

body.question: Is the verb describing the subject, or saying how something was done?

options.label: linking, so a plain describing word
options.use_it_when: The word after the verb tells you what the subject is or is like.

options.label: acting, so an *-ly* word
options.use_it_when: The word after the verb tells you how the action was carried out.

b.means: People joined it a few at a time.
They were moving round in the wind.

a.means: It looked like a bad problem.
There is a damp smell in there.

b.text: The kitchen smells strongly of paint.
b.means: The paint smell in there is powerful.

body.deciding_factor: Ask whether the word after the verb describes the subject. If it does, the *-ly* ending has to go.
body.trap: You were taught that describing words go with nouns and *-ly* words go with verbs. That splits the world in the wrong place, because a linking verb is followed by a description of the subject.
body.register_note: Both belong everywhere. The choice shows up most in Speaking Part 2, where *it looked amazing* and *it sounded strange* are constant.

body.text: The rule for what follows a linking verb
After one of the fourteen linking verbs, use a plain describing word. The *-ly* form belongs after an action verb.

body.lead_in: Four linking verbs, each followed by a plain describing word.

items.text: The rules remain unclear for part-time students.
items.gloss: Nobody has explained them properly.

items.text: The milk in the fridge has gone sour.
items.gloss: It is no longer safe to drink.

items.text: The applicants stayed calm during the delay.
items.gloss: Nobody got upset while they waited.

items.text: The estimate seems low for a job this size.
items.gloss: It looks as though it will cost more.

body.so_what: Not one of them takes an *-ly* ending, and every one describes the subject.

body.text: Two orders for a verb with two things after it
*Give*, *send*, *show*, *offer* and *lend* allow both orders. *Explain*, *describe*, *suggest*, *mention* and *report* allow only one. This is fixed for each verb.

body.caption: Some verbs give you a choice of order; some give you one.
rows: gave the form to the office
sent a notice to the tenants
explained the change to the staff
described the route to the group
suggested a date to the panel
footnotes: The dashes are not gaps in the language. Those three verbs have no person-first order at all.

body.text: Three errors from getting the class wrong

body.wrong: Traffic on the bypass has become seriously.
body.right: Traffic on the bypass has become serious.
body.why_it_happens: *Become* is a verb, and *-ly* words are taught as the ones that follow verbs. *Become* links the subject to a description, so the description has no ending.
body.smallest_fix: Take the *-ly* off anything following *be*, *become*, *seem*, *look*, *feel*, *stay* or *remain*.

body.wrong: The accident was happened at the junction.
body.right: The accident happened at the junction.
body.why_it_happens: The sentence describes something the subject did not choose, and that feels like something being done to it. Only a verb that takes an object can be turned round this way.
body.smallest_fix: Ask *what?* after the verb. No answer means no *was* form: *happened*, *occurred*, *arrived*.

body.wrong: I really enjoyed during the placement.
body.right: I really enjoyed the placement.
body.why_it_happens: *Enjoy* feels like *relax*, which needs nothing after it. *Enjoy* always takes an object, even when it is only *it* or *myself*.
body.smallest_fix: Add the thing that was enjoyed straight after the verb.

body.heard: An adverb describes a verb, so after a verb you use the *-ly* word.
body.truth: That holds for action verbs and fails for the fourteen linking verbs. In *the results look bad*, the word describes the results, not the looking, so it takes no ending.
body.what_to_do: Learn the fourteen. After any of them, ask what is being described, and use the plain word when the answer is the subject.

body.mechanism: Arabic builds a passive shape from most verbs regularly, so the pattern is easy to extend to English verbs that take no object.
body.wrong: Three deliveries were arrived this morning.
body.right: Three deliveries arrived this morning.
body.fix: Only verbs that can take an object have this form. *Arrive*, *happen* and *sleep* do not.

body.headline: Ask *what?* after the verb. No answer means no object.

articles.title: The order English puts things in

article_json.also_called: Canonical word order, adverbial position, verb–object adjacency and inversion
article_json.one_line: This explains why English order is fixed where other languages are free, and names the four places it flips.
article_json.short_answer: Subject, verb, object, and nothing between the verb and the object. Extra parts go after the object or at the front.
article_json.question_in_learner_words: Why can't I move the words around?

body.text: Order is what English uses instead of endings
Many languages put an ending on each word to show its job. Once the endings are there, the words can move about and the meaning holds.
English dropped almost all of those endings. Position took over the job, so the order is not a style preference. It is what tells your reader who did what.

body.lead_in: The same three words, in two orders. Nothing else changes.

items.text: The inspector questioned the driver.
items.gloss: The driver was the one answering questions.

items.text: The driver questioned the inspector.
items.gloss: Now the inspector is the one answering.

items.text: The storm damaged the sea wall.
items.gloss: The wall is broken and the storm did it.

items.text: It's the wall that's damaged, not the road.
items.gloss: The road is fine. The wall is the problem.

body.so_what: Swapping the two names swapped who did it. No word changed shape.

body.text: Nothing comes between a verb and its object
The object sits against its verb. Every extra part waits until after the object.
One rule covers a whole family of errors that other books treat one at a time. If the object is there, nothing gets in front of it.

body.lead_in: Three kinds of extra part, all pushed out to the far side of the object.

items.text: She speaks Portuguese very well.
items.gloss: Her Portuguese is strong.

items.text: We reviewed the applications carefully.
items.gloss: Nobody rushed through them.

items.text: The team finished the survey on Thursday.
items.gloss: Thursday was the last day of the work.

body.so_what: In each one the object touches the verb, and the extra part sits behind it.

body.text: The order two or three extra parts take

body.caption: How, then where, then when. That is the usual order.
footnotes: Full sentence: *They worked quietly in the back office all morning.*
Any of the three can move to the front instead, and then it comes first.

body.lead_in: Two extra parts at a time, in the order the table gives.
body.dimension: the order of two extra parts

items.text: The results were published online last Friday.
items.gloss: You could see them on a website from Friday.

items.text: We met at the depot on Tuesday.
items.gloss: Tuesday was the day, and the depot was the place.

items.text: They cycle to the campus every day.
items.gloss: It is how they get in each morning.

body.so_what: Where comes before when in all three. Reversing it sounds wrong to a reader.

body.text: Four places where the order flips

body.gloss: putting the helping verb in front of the subject

show_first.text: Has the committee published the figures?
Never before had the service been so unreliable.
Had the funding arrived earlier, the work would be finished.

body.name_line: That flip is called **inversion**.
body.anchor_line: One mechanism, three uses. The helping verb steps in front of the subject and nothing else moves.

body.lead_in: The order flips in four places and nowhere else:
items: in a question: *Have the trains started running?*
after a negative word at the front: *Never had the queue been so long.*
in a formal *if*-sentence with *if* removed: *Had we known, we would have waited.*
after *so* and *neither* in a short reply: *So did we.*

body.text: The second and third are formal and risky, and they are covered where they belong. The point here is that all four are one mechanism, not four rules.
Three errors that come from moving words

body.wrong: She speaks very well Portuguese.
body.right: She speaks Portuguese very well.
body.why_it_happens: The describing part belongs to the verb, so it feels natural to keep it next to the verb. English keeps the object next to the verb instead.
body.smallest_fix: Move the describing part to the end, behind the object.

body.wrong: We met on Tuesday at the depot.
body.right: We met at the depot on Tuesday.
body.why_it_happens: Several languages put the time first because it sets the scene. English works outwards from the action, so the place comes before the time.
body.smallest_fix: Put where before when, or move the time part to the front of the sentence.

body.wrong: Could you tell me where is the registration office?
body.right: Could you tell me where the registration office is?
body.why_it_happens: The sentence is a question overall, so the flipped order feels required all the way through. Only the outer question flips; the part inside goes back to normal order.
body.smallest_fix: Put the subject back in front of the verb after *where*, *what*, *how* or *why*.

body.heard: English word order is subject, verb, object, and it never changes.
body.truth: It holds for ordinary statements, and it flips in four named places: questions, after a negative word at the front, in a formal *if*-sentence, and after *so* or *neither*. Everywhere else it holds.
body.what_to_do: Use the normal order unless you are doing one of those four things. The flip is a device, not a free choice.

body.mechanism: Tamil puts the verb at the end of the sentence, and endings on the words show which one is the doer.
body.wrong: The council the parking charges last month increased.
body.right: The council increased the parking charges last month.
body.fix: Put the verb straight after the subject, then the object, then the time.

body.mechanism: Chinese puts the time and place in front of the verb, so those parts naturally land between the subject and the verb.
body.wrong: The engineers at the depot on Monday checked the pumps.
body.right: The engineers checked the pumps at the depot on Monday.
body.fix: Keep the subject, verb and object together. Send time and place to the end.
